strengths: Well-motivated and practically important problem: the paper targets a genuine deployment gap in V2X cooperative perception (system-level latency, memory, and bandwidth of FP32 intermediate fusion), which most prior work ignores.

First fully quantized end-to-end multi-agent intermediate fusion system; the system-level framing (local inference + communication + fusion latency) is more meaningful for real deployment than idealized accuracy comparisons.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: three datasets (DAIR-V2X, V2X-Real, OPV2V), multiple fusion methods (Pyramid Fusion, F-Cooper, AttFuse, V2X-ViT, Who2com, Where2comm), INT4/8 and 8/8 settings, robustness under pose noise, comparison with PTQ baselines (PD-Quant, LiDAR-PTQ), and ablations on calibration data size/steps and codebook hyperparameters.

Genuine hardware-based system evaluation on a real ROS/TensorRT deployment platform (V2X-ReaLO), including measured latency breakdown (Fig. 5), power/energy measurements (Table 9), and edge-platform testing; this substantially exceeds what most quantization papers provide.

Honest limitation discussion (e.g., severe degradation of V2X-ViT under aggressive quantization, absence of 2-bit experiments with a reasoned justification) and a commitment to public release, supporting reproducibility.

Reasonable attribution: the PTQ pipeline is explicitly built on established techniques (AdaRound, block-wise reconstruction, LiDAR-PTQ ideas, codebook messaging related to CodeFilling), with the contribution framed as the system integration and multi-agent-specific alignment rather than a fundamentally new quantization algorithm.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty in individual components: the PTQ recipe (max-min init, learnable rounding, block-wise reconstruction) closely follows prior work, and codebook-based messaging overlaps substantially with CodeFilling (Hu et al., 2024); the main new technical pieces (KL-based heterogeneity alignment and L2 spatial alignment losses) are simple and evaluated only empirically. The contribution is primarily applied/systems, which is acceptable but lowers the technical depth relative to the claims of a 'novel alignment module'.

The headline +9.5 mAP30 gain over full-precision systems is largely an artifact of the latency-constrained evaluation setting (full-precision suffers more under simulated communication delay), not of superior perception; under ideal conditions QuantV2X slightly underperforms the full-precision upper bound. The paper states this, but the abstract could be read as an absolute accuracy improvement.

System-level performance numbers depend on a simulated communication model (fixed 27 Mbps rate, uniform 0-200 ms asynchrony) rather than measured over-the-air V2X links; the latency measurements use an RTX 3090 / A6000 class GPU, which weakens the edge-deployment claims. The promised Cellular-V2X testbed evaluation is left to future work.

Inconsistencies between model-level and system-level settings: the abstract/introduction emphasize INT4 results, but the system-level experiments use INT8 only, making the strongest claims not directly aligned with the deployed system; the mAP30 metric choice (IoU 0.30) is unusually lenient.

Some technical presentations are imprecise: the bandwidth formula 'log2(H × W × C × 32/8)' is dimensionally incorrect (the bandwidth should be H×W×C×32/8 bits, without log2), and the α_r combination weights in Eq. (2) are never specified how they are obtained or trained.

The 3.2× system latency speedup aggregates different components with different speedups (1.6× local, 5.3× transmission, 2.5× fusion); the transmission speedup of 5.3× is dominated by the message-size reduction, which is a straightforward consequence of transmitting code indices rather than a novel result.

No discussion of codebook generalization across scenes/agents (e.g., whether a codebook learned on one dataset or agent configuration transfers), and only single-frame settings are evaluated despite claims about storing historical BEV features.

strengths: Genuine system-level contribution: the paper goes beyond simulation and provides end-to-end latency, bandwidth, memory, and power measurements from real hardware (TensorRT/ROS on edge platforms), which is rare in cooperative perception research and directly relevant to deployment.

Comprehensive and well-structured evaluation: model-level results across multiple datasets (DAIR-V2X, V2X-Real, OPV2V), multiple fusion methods, and multiple collaboration modes (heterogeneous LiDAR/camera agents), plus ablations on calibration data size, steps, codebook size (nC, nR), and comparisons against PD-Quant and LiDAR-PTQ.

System-level evaluation protocol that models latency under realistic asynchronous conditions (Tcomm with transmission rate and delay distribution) is a meaningful way to compare methods, and the results (Table 3) show quantization enabling a system to win under latency constraints where the ideal-accuracy ranking would differ.
Honest and reasonably detailed limitations discussion (e.g., V2X-ViT degradation under quantization, 2-bit impracticality), and commitment to open-source release.

Clear positioning of the problem: the three-component latency decomposition (local, communication, fusion) and the demonstration that quantization helps all three simultaneously is a useful framing for the field.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The individual components are largely assembled from existing work: max-min calibration, AdaRound rounding (Nagel et al., 2020), block-wise reconstruction (BRECQ-style, Li et al., 2021a), and codebook-index message transmission, which closely resembles CodeFilling (Hu et al., 2024). The so-called 'novel alignment module' is essentially standard distillation losses (KL divergence on features, L2 on boxes) applied during PTQ calibration. As an Applied/Systems contribution this could be acceptable, but the paper repeatedly overclaims novelty ('first work', 'novel codebook learning') rather than positioning itself honestly as a systems integration of known techniques.

Technical errors in the communication-cost analysis (Sec. 2.3.1). The bandwidth of a BEV feature is stated as log2(H×W×C×32/8) and the codebook alternative as log2(H×W×log2(nL)×nR/8); the correct sizes are H×W×C×32/8 bytes and H×W×log2(nL)×nR/8 bytes, respectively — taking log2 of the byte count is mathematically wrong and inflates the claimed reduction. While the qualitative conclusion survives, an error of this kind in a core motivation section undermines confidence.

Inconsistencies between claims and settings. The abstract headlines INT4 weight / INT8 activation accuracy preservation, but the system-level experiments (the basis for the headline ×3.2 latency and +9.5 mAP30 numbers) use INT8/INT8 only. The '+9.5 mAP30 over full-precision baselines' is an artifact of latency-constrained evaluation and should not be presented as an accuracy improvement without immediate qualification. Terminology also wavers between AP30, mAP30, and '99.8% of accuracy' claims.

Key methodological details are underspecified: Eq. (2) introduces combination weights αr for multi-code reconstruction but never defines how they are computed or trained; the text mentions a 'product-quantized codebook' but no product-quantization structure (sub-vector partitioning) is actually described; calibration for multi-agent combinations (Algorithm 1) lacks the pseudo-code granularity to verify the heterogeneity/spatial alignment losses are applied consistently.

Sparse and sometimes noisy evidence for the strongest claims. Fig. 6 (scaling under GPU budgets) has small axis labels and no numbers, making the scaling argument hard to verify; the +220.5%/+13.1% motivation figures in Fig. 1 are not traceable to any table. The robustness analysis (Fig. 4) covers only pose noise on one collaboration mode of one dataset.

Some headline framing is misleading: 'first fully quantized multi-agent system' is asserted repeatedly, but prior work already partially quantizes V2X pipelines (Zhou et al., 2024a) and CodeFilling uses codebook-based messages; the delta is end-to-end coverage rather than a fundamentally new capability. Given the assembled nature of the contribution, the paper would benefit from more rigorous verification (error analysis, seeds, statistical significance), none of which is provided.

strengths: Strong practical relevance: the paper addresses a genuine gap between accuracy-oriented cooperative perception research and real-world deployability, and the Applied/Systems contribution is well matched to the evidence provided.

Impressive system-level evaluation: latency is measured on actual hardware (ROS + TensorRT on edge platforms with custom CUDA kernels), with a clear decomposition into local inference, communication, and fusion latency (Fig. 5), plus power/energy measurements (Table 9). This goes well beyond the usual FLOPs-only efficiency reporting.

Comprehensive experimental coverage across three datasets (DAIR-V2X, V2X-Real, OPV2V), six fusion methods, multiple bit configurations (INT4/8 and INT8/8), ablations on calibration data size and steps, comparisons with PTQ baselines (PD-Quant, LiDAR-PTQ), and robustness analysis under pose noise.

The motivation that quantization enables larger-capacity models under tight memory budgets (Section 3.3, Fig. 6) is an interesting and underexplored argument, and the +9.5 mAP30 gain over full-precision baselines under latency constraints is a compelling system-level result even if per-component accuracy is only comparable.

The identification of quantization-specific failure modes in multi-agent fusion (heterogeneous activation statistics across agents, spatial misalignment) is a genuine insight, and the two alignment losses are simple, targeted, and validated by ablation (Table 2: recovery from 97.4% to 98.8% of full precision).
Reproducibility is supported by use of the open HEAL repository, V2X-ReaLO platform, stated calibration protocol (0.5% data, 5k steps), and a stated intent to open-source the system.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty on the components: the PTQ pipeline is largely a composition of established techniques (max-min calibration, scale search à la EasyQuant/BRECQ, AdaRound rounding, block-wise reconstruction), and the codebook-based message transmission is very close to CodeFilling (Hu et al., 2024). The main contribution is the integration and deployment engineering, which is valuable for an Applied/Systems paper, but reviewers should not expect new algorithmic machinery.

A likely error in the bandwidth formula (Section 2.3.1): the original bandwidth is written as log2(H×W×C×32/8), which is a logarithm of the byte count rather than the byte count itself; the comparison ratios between the two formulas remain plausible but the expression as stated is dimensionally incorrect and should be fixed.

A consistency concern in the 'fully quantized' claim: model-level results emphasize INT4 weights, but the system-level evaluation (the headline ×3.2 latency and +9.5 mAP30 results) uses INT8/INT8. The strongest accuracy-preservation claim (99.8%) and the strongest efficiency claim are thus not demonstrated under the same setting, and the INT4 system-level latency/accuracy is not reported.

The system-level mAP advantage over full-precision baselines is partly attributable to quantization enabling larger models under memory budgets (Section 3.3) rather than quantization itself; the confound between bit-width and model capacity in Table 3 is not fully disentangled.

The KL-based heterogeneity loss and L2 spatial loss are formulated loosely (e.g., KL between BEV feature maps treated as distributions; L2 over 'bounding box distributions' without defining the representation), and the interaction between the alignment losses during the calibration loop (Algorithm 1) is described at a level that would make exact reimplementation difficult without the released code.

Some important analyses are relegated to the supplementary material (per-fusion quantization analysis, codebook nC/nR ablation, latency across fusion methods), which weakens the main-text narrative; the scaling argument in Fig. 6 is only shown as a single plot without accompanying numbers or backbone specifications.

Robustness to communication latency is simulated with an idealized model (fixed 27 Mbps rate plus uniform 0-200 ms delay); the conclusion appropriately acknowledges that a real Cellular-V2X testbed evaluation is left to future work, so 'real-world deployment' claims should be read with some caution.

strengths: Timely and practically significant problem: the paper targets the well-argued gap between accuracy-centric cooperative perception research and real-world deployability (memory, latency, bandwidth), which is a genuine and underexplored direction for the community.

Strong systems-level evidence appropriate for an Applied/Systems contribution: latency is profiled end-to-end (T_local, T_comm, T_fus) on a TensorRT/ROS deployment stack rather than simulated FLOPs, with a latency decomposition analysis (Fig. 6) that cleanly disentangles model-side vs. communication-side gains, and additional real-platform evaluation on V2X-ReaLO plus power/energy measurements.

Comprehensive and mostly convincing experiments: results across three datasets (DAIR-V2X, V2X-Real, OPV2V), six fusion architectures, multiple bit configurations (INT8 and INT4/8), comparisons against PTQ baselines (PD-Quant, LiDAR-PTQ), communication baselines (Where2Comm, CodeFilling), robustness to pose noise, calibration-size/step ablations, codebook (n_L, n_R) ablations, and qualitative results. The V2X-ReaLO online results (Table 12) showing the quantized system outperforming the full-precision online system are a compelling demonstration.

The proposed alignment module (heterogeneity KL alignment + spatial bounding-box alignment during calibration) addresses a real, V2X-specific quantization failure mode (cross-agent activation heterogeneity and spatial misalignment), and Table 10/11 plus D.5 carefully disentangle its role from AdaRound.

Reproducibility commitment: the system builds on the open-source HEAL codebase and the open V2X-ReaLO platform, with a stated public release; hyperparameters, calibration settings, and hardware details are reported.
Clear positioning and honest scoping: the appendix (2-bit discussion, fusion-method-specific degradation analysis e.g. V2X-ViT) acknowledges limitations candidly rather than overclaiming.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: the components are largely assembled from established techniques (max-min calibration, scale search, AdaRound-style rounding, BRECQ-style block reconstruction, codebook messaging closely following CodeFilling [13], Gumbel-Softmax quantization). The main novelty is the system integration and two relatively simple alignment losses; the paper is best viewed as Applied/Systems rather than a new-method contribution, and the individual technical pieces are incremental.

Internal tension in the 'fully quantized / PTQ' framing: the codebook learning stage (Section 2.3, Appendix E.4) performs joint retraining of encoder, fusion, head, and codebook for 10 additional epochs with quantization in the loop, which is quantization-aware training rather than pure post-training quantization; the full-precision baselines do not receive the same benefit. The headline '+9.5 mAP30' also conflates quantization gains with the codebook-compression gains already established by CodeFilling, although the decomposition analysis (Fig. 6) partially mitigates this concern.

Some baseline comparisons appear potentially favorable to the method: Table 3's full-precision baseline transmits 8.6 MB uncompressed, while compressed variants and QuantV2X operate at very different message sizes (0.03 MB); a fairer accuracy-vs-bandwidth Pareto comparison at matched bitrates would strengthen the claims. The simulated system-latency experiments use a simplified uniform asynchrony model (U(0,200ms)) rather than measured delays for some configurations.

Inconsistencies and minor soundness gaps: the model-level experiments use INT4/8 while system-level uses INT8/8 (bit setting changes between headline claims); in Table 2, AdaRound alone degrades AP30 below the max-min baseline for LP+CR, which is unexplained; Eq. (9) applies KL divergence directly to continuous fused feature maps without defining the distributions being compared; and the spatial alignment loss (Eq. 10) matching predictions between FP and quantized models on calibration data may propagate full-precision spatial biases rather than ground truth.

Latency measurements average only 10 runs on an RTX 3090, which is not a typical in-vehicle GPU; although Appendix E discusses edge platforms and Fig. 7 addresses memory budgets, primary latency numbers come from a desktop GPU, slightly weakening the deployment claim.

Several key details are deferred or underspecified in the main text (codebook product-quantization structure, how the alignment module is instantiated architecturally vs. purely as losses, TensorRT plug-in details), which may hinder exact reproducibility despite the release commitment.

strengths: The paper targets a genuinely under-explored and practically important problem: system-level deployability of cooperative V2X perception, rather than purely accuracy-driven benchmarking. Framing evaluation around latency, memory budgets, and communication volume is a valuable reframing.

The evaluation is unusually thorough for a systems claim: latency decomposition into local inference, communication, and fusion stages (Fig. 5, Fig. 6), measurement on a real ROS/TensorRT testbed (V2X-ReaLO), power consumption analysis, and scaling-under-memory-budget experiments (Fig. 7).

Extensive ablations are provided, including calibration dataset size/steps, codebook size (nL, nR), robustness to pose noise across distance ranges, per-distance/per-IoU breakdowns (Table 10), and discussion of when AdaRound vs. the alignment module matter (D.5).
The paper is honest about failure modes, e.g., the substantial degradation of V2X-ViT and F-Cooper under quantization (D.3), and the infeasibility of 2-bit quantization for this domain (Appendix C).

The V2X-ReaLO online results (Table 12) show the quantized system outperforming the online full-precision system across collaboration modes, which is a convincing demonstration that latency, not raw precision, dominates in deployment.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The work is largely a well-engineered combination of existing techniques: AdaRound [28], BRECQ-style block-wise reconstruction [18], max-min/scale-search calibration, codebook-based communication from CodeFilling [13] and deep-compression lineage [10], and Gumbel-Softmax product quantization. The core new component is the alignment loss (L_hetero + L_spatial), and Table 11 shows the alignment module adds only +0.3/+0.7 AP on top of naive rounding, suggesting the headline results are driven mostly by standard PTQ machinery.

Inconsistent quantization settings weaken the headline claims. The model-level study is INT4/8, but the system-level experiments that produce the headline '3.2x latency reduction' and '+9.5 mAP30' are INT8/8 only. The abstract blends these without clearly separating them, and INT4/8 system-level results are never reported. The +9.5 mAP30 gain is a latency-induced effect, not a perception-accuracy gain, yet is presented alongside accuracy claims in a way that could mislead.

Generalization of the PTQ method is incomplete: Table 1 shows severe collapse for attention-based fusion (V2X-ViT drops from 57.4 to 29.9 AP30 at 4/8, i.e., ~48% loss), so the claim that the method generalizes across fusion methods holds mainly for CNN/convolutional architectures. The paper acknowledges this but does not resolve it.

Several results are under-explained: calibration with 20,000 steps performs worse than 5,000 steps (Table 7) with no analysis; the component-stacking in Table 2 is ambiguous (the final row does not make clear whether L_hetero and L_spatial are combined, and the reported final number matches the '+L_spatial'-only row); QuantV2X's margin over LiDAR-PTQ is 0.4 AP30 at comparable cost (Table 4), which is within plausible run-to-run variance and no error bars or multiple seeds are reported anywhere.

The codebook communication component substantially overlaps CodeFilling [13] (same 0.03 MB payload, same codebook messaging idea); the delta over that baseline in Table 3 (51.4 to 52.6 mAP30) is modest, and the contribution of the quantization-aware codebook training versus simply applying CodeFilling in the quantized system is not isolated.

Reproducibility is a concern: the system is only promised for release ('will be publicly released'), the paper depends on custom CUDA kernels/TensorRT plug-ins that are non-trivial to replicate, and key hyperparameters (alpha, beta, T for scale search, lambda_rec) are not specified. The camera-based agent (C_R with Lift-Splat-Shoot + ResNet50) is quantized but camera-only quantization results are not broken out.

Clarity issues: the bandwidth formula in Section 2.3 (log2 of byte counts) is dimensionally odd and essentially a log of size rather than a meaningful bandwidth expression; Fig. 3's qualitative claims are hard to verify at the shown resolution; Appendix B/C are written as a Q&A that, while useful, pads the paper rather than strengthening the technical argument.

The 'first fully quantized multi-agent system' novelty claim is asserted repeatedly but defended only by citation-gap reasoning; given the close relationship to CodeFilling plus standard PTQ, the claim of a fundamentally new direction is overstated relative to what is technically demonstrated.

strengths: Strong system-level framing: the paper moves beyond accuracy-only evaluation to deployment-oriented metrics (local inference latency, communication latency, fusion latency, memory budgets, power consumption), which is genuinely valuable for the cooperative perception field and is well aligned with an Applied/Systems contribution type.

Comprehensive experimental evidence: evaluations span three datasets (DAIR-V2X, V2X-Real, OPV2V), multiple fusion architectures (Pyramid Fusion, F-Cooper, AttFuse, V2X-ViT, Who2com, Where2comm), heterogeneous agent settings (LiDAR-LiDAR and LiDAR-camera), pose-noise robustness studies, and a real-world ROS-based deployment on the V2X-ReaLO platform (Table 12). The latency decomposition analysis (Fig. 5, Fig. 6) convincingly disentangles model-side vs. communication-side gains.

The headline result is compelling and well-supported: a 3.2x system-level latency reduction with higher mAP30 than the full-precision baseline under realistic latency constraints (Table 3), approaching the ideal upper-bound (52.6 vs. 53.8), demonstrates that quantization-enabled timeliness outweighs minor precision loss.

Good ablation coverage: the role of the alignment module vs. AdaRound is carefully analyzed (Tables 2, 10, 11), calibration dataset size/steps are ablated, codebook hyperparameters (nL, nR) are studied, and 2-bit quantization is explicitly discussed as impractical rather than silently omitted.

Transparent attribution and release commitment: the paper clearly credits AdaRound, LiDAR-PTQ, CodeFilling, HEAL, and V2X-ReaLO, includes an LLM-usage statement, and promises public release, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Novelty is primarily integrative rather than algorithmic: the core PTQ machinery (max-min calibration, scale search, AdaRound, block-wise reconstruction, codebook messaging closely related to CodeFilling [13] and Deep Compression [10]) is largely adapted from prior work. The genuinely new pieces are the heterogeneity/spatial alignment losses and the system integration; the contribution should be judged as a systems paper, and on that basis it is acceptable, but the methodological novelty is modest.

Minor inconsistency in bit configurations: the model-level experiments (Sections 3.1, Tables 1-2) use INT4/8, while the system-level experiments (Section 3.2) use INT8/8 'to be consistent with the previous protocol'. The abstract's headline claims mix both settings without clearly flagging this, which weakens the narrative coherence of the 'fully quantized' story.

The system-level performance gains depend on a simulated latency model (Tcomm = fs/v + U(0,200ms), 27 Mbps) rather than end-to-end measured delays for all baselines; while the protocol follows prior work and a real testbed experiment is included, the comparison with CodeFilling and Where2Comm under this model would be stronger with measured rather than formula-derived communication latency for each system.

Some results are under-explained: in Table 12 the quantized online system substantially outperforms the full-precision online system (e.g., V2I pedestrian 32.9 vs. 27.7) and in some cells approaches or exceeds ideal full-precision; the offered explanation (memory enabling larger feature banks) is plausible but qualitative and unverified by measurement. Table 2 also shows +Lhetero alone exceeding +Lspatial inconsistently across modes, which deserves clarification.

The stated 'first fully quantized multi-agent system' claim should be softened; related single-agent LiDAR-PTQ and communication-codebook works cover substantial portions of the design space, and 'fully quantized' here means INT8/8 in system experiments (not INT4, which is only demonstrated model-level without the compressor).

Writing has minor issues: broken/placeholder URL in reference 10, some notation inconsistencies, and heavy reliance on the appendix for key details (testing environments, PTQ baselines), which reduces readability of the main text.
